utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Would the Registrar call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is Case Number IT-03-68-PT, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Would both parties make their appearances. We have a lot today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour. My name is Jan Wubben for the Prosecution team, together with my co-counsels, Patricia Sellers, Jayantha Jayasuriya, Kristina Carey, and our case manager, Diane Boles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I am Vasvija Vidovic, together with Mr. John Jones. I represent Mr. Naser Oric. And with us today we have Mr. Geoff Roberts, our case manager. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Vidovic. As I remember it, this is the third conference, held in accordance with Rule 65 bis. And I note that already a year has passed since the indictment against this accused was filed, so I think this coming Sunday is an anniversary. And to begin, I note that the Chamber received the pre-trial briefs from both parties. They were timely filed, and I thank the parties for their complying with the deadlines. Well, moving on to pending motions, I know that there is one, which is the -- which is from the Prosecution, requesting leave to add three witnesses to its list of witnesses. And I also note that the Defence does not oppose the motion. So I would say they were so added in its list, but however it is still for the Trial Chamber at the time of Pre-trial Conference whether to limit the overall number of witnesses or not. But as the pre-trial Judge, I like to confirm with the Defence that they indeed received the added -- the statements of the witnesses which were added recently, even in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have received summaries of the statements. We haven't received the statements themselves. However, the Prosecution has informed us that they will be available to us before the 10th of April, and we have agreed with that. And this refers both to the English version and the B/C/S version of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So there's no problem for the Prosecution to disclose them by 10th of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 10th of April being Saturday, so 9th of April is okay or 12th of April, being Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Please, if possible, Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be so ordered. In terms of a disclosure pursuant to Rule 66(A)(i) and (A)(ii), is there anything to raise for the Prosecution? Are they completed? Rule 66(A)(i) and (ii) disclosure?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, they are completed; however, I would like -- I requested Mr. Jayasuriya to address this issue. May I refer to him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jayasuriya.

utterances.speaker: MR. JAYASURIYA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. 66(A)(i) disclosure has been completed, and 66(A)(ii), except for one item. All the other statements have been disclosed to the Defence. The item that is outstanding is the B/C/S version of the James Gow transcript, where we were informed that unfortunately no B/C/S version was maintained at the time of the Rule 61 hearing, therefore we have taken steps to obtain a translation using the transcripts which is available to the Prosecution or even top the registry, My Lord. So we have already disclosed, or provided the Defence with the English transcript. And the B/C/S translation is expected in mid-April, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could remind me, again, of Mr. James Gow?

utterances.speaker: MR. JAYASURIYA
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. JAYASURIYA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you think it can be completed by middle of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. JAYASURIYA
utterances.text: That's the indication that we have received from the DVIU, which is handling the translations at the moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So do you think I can set the date as by 16th of April, Friday?

utterances.speaker: MR. JAYASURIYA
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jayasuriya.

utterances.speaker: MR. JAYASURIYA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, triggering -- triggered by you addressing the date of the 16th, I see in my agenda at the same time that Monday -- that Monday is a kind of UN holiday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes. That's Easter Monday, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: So if it can be the 13th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 13th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I'm sorry to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for reminding me. I don't expect somebody to file a motion on Easter Monday. Then my understanding is that the Defence has something to raise in relation to Rule 68 disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In terms of disclosure generally, as Your Honour may know, we had a meeting with the Prosecutor yesterday which was pretty fruitful and we discussed a number of disclosure issues. So what I have to say is not necessarily confined to Rule 68. But the chief problem is really the following: Over the last few months we have addressed a number of requests to the Prosecution for disclosure of various items. We have set out categories of material in which we are interested. And it appears that the Prosecution has not been able to conduct a number of those searches because our case doesn't have the requisite priority within the system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's a matter of priority inside the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Inside the Prosecution, or inside the Tribunal. I'm not sure precisely how it works. But, I first -- the main point is that since we don't at this moment have a trial date, it's very difficult for those requests to be granted priority. So one thing I wanted to suggest to Your Honour is given, as Your Honour noted, that it's been one year since Mr. Oric was arrested and he's been in custody for a year, since we're aiming to have this case, or the intent was to have this case trial-ready, whether Your Honour would be able to set a trial date or give some indication which would enable these requests to be treated as a matter of priority, because there are a number of outstanding requests and it's really extremely important that we have those documents. There is another matter relating to UNHCR documents, but perhaps I'll address Your Honour on that in a moment. That's a separate issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm very pleased to hear that from the Defence. I'm pleased to say that this case is moving steadfastly towards being ready for the start of the trial. Although, I cannot give the parties an estimate as to when the trial may actually begin, I can say this: The pre-trial progress and its readiness for trial are being regularly discussed among the Chambers. So we can give an estimate in one way or another in due course. So the Chamber will bear in mind the necessity to set a date as soon as possible. Having said that, is there any comment from the Prosecution in relation to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Well, I can confirm what my learned colleague to you revealed as a kind of cooperation in a constructive way, together with Defence counsel. And indeed I can also confirm that when it comes to priorities, we don't have a trial date as such, and that means that whenever other Trial Chambers schedule their trial, that it's a natural way of speeding up trials to meet in advance the disclosure obligations. So setting a date for trial is very productive by advocating our priorities among the others in the queue for the disclosure searches. So I will indeed be grateful if Chambers at some time in due course can set or schedule some date on whatever condition it can be done. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Wubben. Can I take it then that both parties are ready to start the trial at any moment from now? Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's something of a chicken-and-egg problem, in that we would be trial-ready when we have the documents which we require, in particular many of the categories of documents which we're seeking disclosure of. The problem really, which I was bringing to Your Honour's attention, is that until we have a trial date a few months in the future, we're not going to have those disclosure requests. We're not -- I certainly wouldn't suggest that we're ready to go to trial at any moment precisely because we don't have these main documents that we need. What would be helpful is if a tentative date was set, let's say, in August or September, then we could proceed. Having said that, we're not far off being trial-ready, I don't know if it's worth giving an estimate, but certainly in a month or so we would certainly be ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That is helpful. Thank you. Let's go back to the number of witnesses. So the number of witnesses which was originally planned by the Prosecution is 57, I guess, and seven of which are 92 bis witnesses. So that -- my understanding is that the Prosecution wishes to call the 50 witnesses live. Is that correct, including the three which were added recently?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I will give the floor to Mr. Jayantha Jayasuriya for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jayasuriya.

utterances.speaker: MR. JAYASURIYA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, about the 92 bis statements, as the Chamber has already been informed, I believe the Defence has indicated their concern to admit one of those witnesses as 92 bis witnesses. So therefore, at a future date there will have to be an addition by the Trial Chamber whether it permits the Prosecution to admit the rest of the witnesses as 92 bis witnesses. Subject to that, Your Honour, the Prosecution wishes to leave all other witnesses as live witnesses who are currently listed in the 65 ter filings. But the Prosecution is trying its best to adopt the 89(F) procedure with regard to at least a few of the witnesses and shorten the time that the Prosecution would require for the examination-in-chief of those witnesses and thereby trying to maintain the time frame that it had indicated to the Trial Chamber. So this estimate is currently based on the number that these included in the 65 ter filings, as we left the three witnesses whom Your Honour permitted us to add to the list of witnesses today. But to indicate that the Prosecution is still conducting its investigation then, gathering some more witness statements, and we intend filing the necessary motions in the near future, seeking permission to add those witnesses. But in the Prosecution's estimate, these witnesses would not substantially Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. change the length that is anticipated by the Prosecution. Maybe it might be exceeded, or if may have to increase the time period by about another 20 working hours or so, which comes to about maybe one and a half weeks' time, you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The issue of 89(F), utilising the regime of Rule 89(F) was the topic I was about to raise. Of course the Defence should have a say in relation to this. But speaking from my personal experience, it will help the parties to save time and concentrate on more important issues during the trial. I would like to very much encourage you to utilise that regime as much as possible. So it's better if you could clarify the issues and itemise the issues in relation to this. Does the Defence wish to make a comment on this. Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would just like to say that the Defence has accepted a -- one 92 bis statement, and that it has asked to be able to cross-examine all the other witnesses, in keeping with Rule 92 bis. I believe that my learned friend Jayasuriya has said something else. But this is by way of clarification. We accept one witness in keeping with Rule 92 bis. And for the others, we want to cross-examine them, in keeping with the submission that we have sent to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Vidovic. The regime I mentioned, i.e., Rule 89(F) is the system in which some background facts are adduced in written form and with this witness being subject to the cross-examination. So of course the Defence will be given an opportunity to consent or not, and also given the opportunity to cross-examine. So it's too early to say, but there will -- I think there will be no great harm to the Defence. And then, if Mr. Jones can comment on the issue proposed earlier, which is an organisation, UN organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I'm obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And it can be dealt with in open session, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's really a matter of the UNHCR documents, and it's a matter we highlighted, in fact, in our pre-trial brief at paragraph 17. And essentially the point is this: That these are extremely important documents from our point of view, because the UNHCR documented the situation in the enclave in the relevant period, in detail, and we are seeking to obtain documents from UNHCR. It's a matter which we've been pursuing ourselves with UNHCR and also with the Prosecution, and it's a matter which we discussed with the Prosecution yesterday. And it appears that essentially due to the policy of UNHCR which might be described as somewhat intransigent or inflexible, I don't wish to be unkind to the UNHCR, but certainly it's not easy to obtain documents from them. It's really a matter which we have raised in our pre-trial brief, but I want to reiterate again in the Status Conference, because it may become critical if we're not able to obtain those documents. And one thought which I had was that UNHCR is, after all, a United Nations body, this is a United Nations Tribunal, and perhaps if there's a sufficient groundswell of discontent of obtaining disclosure from UNHCR, perhaps it's a matter that might be addressed by, for example, the President of this Tribunal in a letter to the Secretary-General. I'm not sure. It's something which I just draw to Your Honour's attention at this point in time, because there may be a motion from us on this subject. It may be something which we take up with the President of the Tribunal. But it's of sufficient importance that I thought it should be mentioned today. So it's really simply to put it on the record. It is a problem. We're working with the Prosecution to solve it, and we'll keep Your Honour informed of developments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's see what can be done in relation to this. But it's a long tradition or policy for the institution to maintain such policy. One comment in relation to agreed facts. The Prosecution filed in its annex some agreed facts, but I wonder if there's any possibility to develop further -- i.e., to find more facts which can be agreed upon between the parties. That can be said from the Defence, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, this is something which we also discussed with the Prosecution yesterday, also in terms of stipulations which the Prosecution might make. Our position is that at the present time we're not asking the Prosecution to make any stipulations. The Prosecution has indicated their willingness to stipulate possibly to some of the matters mentioned in our pre-trial brief. But, really, for us it comes to the question, at the moment, of disclosure, because until we have the documents which we require, we won't be in a position really to know whether the stipulations are correct or not. So to give Your Honour an example, the Prosecution might say: "Well, we're willing to stipulate that there was a brigade in this town or a tank on this hill." Until we have the documents, we don't know if that's true. And so for us, stipulations can't substitute for facts, and until we're in a position of having more than the documents that we require, we can't enter into stipulations or accept stipulations from the Prosecution. I don't say that's for all time, but currently, as things stand, we don't seek to make any further admissions and we're not seeking any stipulations from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones. Let me ask some more specific questions, having heard that. If we see the -- like take this one: If we see the suggestion for stipulated facts in the matter, the Prosecution versus Naser Oric, that's the annex of the pre-trial of the Prosecution. And take the first page, the Defence agreed in -- it's A, biographical data, the Defence agreed number 1 to 10, but not 11 and 12. So if we see paragraph 11 and 12, it says: "On 17th of April, 1992, the Potocari Territorial Defence was established. On 17th of April, Mr. Naser Oric became the commander of the TO Potocari." So it is evident that Defence does not agree on these facts, but can I ask why or if you could give some more specific detailed explanation. Of course it is not a compulsory duty on the part of the Defence. So my question is whether you can develop more on agreed facts in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'd take the example you're giving as just a general example. You're not inviting us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- to enter into a detailed discussion of exactly what we agree and disagree with, which is what we've done in our pre-trial brief. And I should also say, I regret I don't have the Prosecution pre-trial brief in front of me, so I've noted what Your Honour has said about paragraph 11. But just looking at that paragraph, the allegation concerns the defendant being the commander of a TO unit. This case is based on command responsibility in Article 7(3) of the Statute, as well as Article 7(1). There are issues of what it precisely means to be a commander, the superior-subordinate position. In other words, that may appear a bland phrase which I take it Your Honour is suggesting we shouldn't have that much difficulty in saying whether or not it's true and perhaps agreeing to it. But in fact that's a matter which contains a great deal -- a great deal of baggage comes with the whole notion of being a commander which is central to this case. For that reason, among others, we didn't admit that paragraph. All I can really say, Your Honour, is that we've considered the matter very seriously and every allegation we didn't agree, we had a good reason for doing so. Of course, we don't wish to appear close-minded. We will consider on what Your Honour has said and have a further look. Would Your Honour mind if I just confer with my colleague?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I am reminded by my learned friends that also there are issues which we have raised on a numerous occasions of authenticity of documents. And a number of these allegations or assertions are based on documentary evidence which we have challenged, and which we have grave doubts about the authenticity of. So that's also behind a lot of the -- I should say, that's a factor which plays heavily in deciding what facts we can admit and which we cannot. I hope that answers Your Honour's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And give thought to my example.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for your comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are there any issues to raise for the parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, when you raised the issue of the annex to our pre-trial brief with the proposals for adjudicated facts, agreed facts, to be specific, it means indeed agreements, so it depends on both parties to settle this agreement. We offered it in our pre-trial brief, and the response was very limited. So this is an opportunity for us to show, whenever Defence counsel offer from their side an opportunity to be open for any raising of issues, again, and topics. We would like to offer those issues and topics, including such an issue as an international armed conflict. This will help us to focus on a trial to speed up and also, of course, to be very effective. And it's good for all parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Nothing from the Defence. Now I would like to ask Mr. Naser Oric directly regarding his health condition and detainment at the Detention Unit. Do you have anything to say, Mr. Oric?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honour, I have nothing to report. Everything is in order; everything is fine. The medicine I receive I use on a regular basis. Everything is in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Then the next Status Conference will be -- should be held before 21st of July, in my calculation. And then we'll consider whether we'll have a pre-trial conference at that time or not, but it remains to be seen. And unless there's anything to be raised --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a matter of whether you would be able to set a trial date or how precisely we would proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's for the Trial Chamber to consider. So we will let you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. I'm obliged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And from our side, the issue still remains that we offer any opportunity that we are available to raise those issues upon agreed facts, so that might be also an opportunity for the Senior Legal Officer at the 65 ter conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Then this hearing is adjourned. ---Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at 3.32 p.m. 24 25
